content.p: In October 1986 a couple living in a house on Moorhouse Street, in the Perth suburb of Willagee, began a run of abductions and killings that lasted just over a month. The press came to call them the Moorhouse murders. David John Birnie and Catherine Birnie held and killed four women. The spree ended on 10 November 1986, when a fifth captive, a 17-year-old, escaped and alerted the authorities, according to PerthNow. The Line-Up and The Canberra Times name her as Kate Moir.

In 2018 the case was part of the debate in Western Australia about parole for the worst offenders. David Birnie died in his prison cell in 2005. Catherine Birnie, the surviving member of the couple, has been refused release at each parole review reported (2007, 2010, 2013 and 2016), and a 2018 bill would let the attorney-general pause those reviews for long periods.

The Sydney Morning Herald reported that in 1985 Catherine had gone to live with David Birnie, leaving her husband and six children behind. She never married him but took his surname. Her youngest son, Peter, was six at the time, and later told Channel Seven's Murder Uncovered that he was "emotionally destroyed" by learning his mother was a serial killer, Yahoo News Australia reported in 2017.

The Line-Up describes David Birnie as working at a business that sold spare parts when the killings began. The couple's house on Moorhouse Street became the centre of the case. The media later called it a "murder chamber", and The Line-Up says two of the victims were buried in Gleneagles National Park after being held in the house.

According to The Line-Up, the first woman taken was Mary Nielson, 22. On 6 October 1986 she was offered cheap tyres for her car and was taken to the Moorhouse Street house. The Line-Up says she was then taken to Gleneagles National Park, where she was killed. The same account says that Susannah Candy, 15, was picked up while hitchhiking on Stirling Highway. The Sydney Morning Herald described the group of victims as three women and a 15-year-old girl taken to the Willagee house.

The Line-Up gives the next victim as Noelene Patterson, 31, whose car had run out of fuel on her way home from work. In its telling, the couple first planned to kill her the same night, but David Birnie kept her for three days. The last of the four dead women named in that account is Denise Brown, 21, who was waiting for a bus. The Line-Up says she was taken into the woods and killed there.

Kate Moir was 17 when she was abducted at knifepoint, according to PerthNow and The Line-Up. Both reports say she got away and that her escape led police to the couple. The Line-Up describes her getting to a nearby shop and then contacting the police, who went on to hear her account of the house. PerthNow quotes former detective Paul Ferguson, the lead investigator, on the Birnies: "They were parasites who lived off each other, the most evil people I've ever, ever come across."

According to the Sydney Morning Herald, the killings ran over five weeks from October into November 1986, with women lured or taken to the house, until a fifth captive got away and raised the alarm. The four dead women were, in that account, raped, stabbed, strangled or clubbed to death.

The Line-Up says David Birnie confessed to the four murders and pleaded guilty at trial. The Sydney Morning Herald wrote in 2010 that he held a life sentence served under strict security for the rape and killing of the victims, and WA Today said in 2013 that the pair were handed strict-security life sentences for the murders.

Catherine Birnie's sentence is described differently. PerthNow said in 2016 that she was held at Bandyup Women's Prison on a life sentence, with a 20-year minimum non-parole period, after the abduction and killing of four women. The Line-Up says she was found guilty and sentenced to four life terms.

Catherine Birnie's first review came in 2007. The Sydney Morning Herald reported in 2010 that the board had assessed her at low risk of reoffending, yet release was refused because her crimes were so extreme. The then attorney-general, Jim McGinty, said she should never be freed, according to PerthNow and WA Today.

In January 2010 the Sydney Morning Herald reported that her next review was due on 5 February. The attorney-general, Christian Porter, continued to support Mr McGinty's decision, and WA Today later reported that Mr Porter decided in March 2010 that she would not be given parole or placed in a re-socialisation program.

In 2013 Attorney-General Michael Mischin accepted a recommendation from the Prisoners Review Board and kept her in prison for a further three years. Tom Percy QC, a prominent Perth lawyer, argued that she should be released. He said that all his information from Bandyup prison was that she was "a little old granny that goes about her work in the library like a church mouse". He added, however, that she "was not the prime mover in it", and that the case had "caught the public attention".

In 2016 Mr Mischin again accepted the board's recommendation not to release her on parole, PerthNow reported. Her next statutory review was then set for 2019. PerthNow also quoted a former detective, the lead investigator Paul Ferguson, who said that he believed Catherine Birnie had never given the victims "one ounce of consideration".

David Birnie was found hanging in his cell at Casuarina Prison, south of Perth, at about 4.30 a.m. on 7 October 2005, according to the Sydney Morning Herald. Police said the circumstances did not appear to be suspicious and that the death would be investigated on behalf of the coroner. The Sydney Morning Herald gave his age as 55; SBS gave it as 54.

The couple had exchanged more than 2,600 letters while both were in custody, but were not allowed any other contact, WA Today reported in 2013. Catherine Birnie was not allowed to attend his funeral, according to the same report.

In October 2018 the state government introduced a bill to parliament that would let the attorney-general order parole authorities to suspend consideration of release for the most serious offenders for up to six years, and extend that suspension by up to six more. Currently, once a minimum term has been served, the Prisoners Review Board decides whether a prisoner can be granted parole, with reviews every three years, the Canberra Times reported.

Attorney-General John Quigley said the policy was meant to reduce trauma for families and friends of murder victims. He said Kate Moir had approached the government to reform the parole laws after a long push that had not succeeded. Mr Quigley said: "We say if there's no prospect of being released on parole, then why should the secondary victims be put through this process every three years?"

The shadow attorney-general, Michael Mischin, questioned whether the bill would deal only with the easiest cases, which the board and the attorney-general would never release anyway. Murdoch University law professor Guy Hall argued that the board already contacted victims' families even where release was not realistically possible, and called parts of the debate grandstanding. Peter McLauchlan, Catherine Birnie's son, backed the planned law, the Canberra Times said.

SBS reported in 2018 that Catherine Birnie, then 66, was due for a parole review the following year. The Canberra Times said that she and William Mitchell, who killed a woman and her three children in Greenough in 1993, were both due for review in 2019.

Catherine Birnie's time in prison has been described in very different terms. Yahoo News Australia reported in 2017 that she had tried to recast herself as a harmless prison librarian, and that she had taken part in a prison production of the musical comedy Nunsense. Her son Peter told Yahoo that he did not want her released and supported the death penalty for her, and when asked what he would say to her, he said: "Hurry up and die. Quickly."

The Line-Up reports that Catherine Birnie is the third woman in Australian history to be marked "never to be released", and credits that status in part to a continuing campaign by Kate Moir. The Line-Up also notes that the pair were tried only for the 1986 murders, and it reports a rumour that they were also responsible for the deaths of two other Perth women who disappeared that year. The same article suggests the 2016 film Hounds of Love may have been inspired by the case.

What the case leaves is a set of facts that are not in doubt: four women dead in a little over a month, a fifth who got away, and two people who each received life sentences. Reports differ on the exact terms of Catherine Birnie's sentence and on David Birnie's age.
